blocks.text: On a limestone ridge some 15 kilometres north-east of Şanlıurfa, in south-eastern Turkey, lies one of the most surprising sites in archaeology: *Göbekli Tepe*, **Potbelly Hill**, usually written as one word in Turkey, *Göbeklitepe*. From about 9600 BCE, more than 11,000 years ago, people here raised huge T-shaped pillars of limestone and set them in round and oval enclosures. The tallest are about 5.5 metres high.

That makes Göbekli Tepe some 6,000 years older than Stonehenge, and UNESCO counts it among the first monumental buildings made by humans. Local Kurdish speakers have their own name for the hill, Girê Mirazan: the hill of wishes.

The builders were hunter-gatherers. Among the remains, archaeologists have found tens of thousands of bones of wild animals, mostly gazelle, and the remains of wild plants, but no domestic animals: farming had not yet begun here. Yet these people quarried, carved and raised stones weighing many tonnes.

Many pillars are carved. Some seem to stand for human figures, with belts and loincloths in low relief; others carry animals: foxes, wild boars, snakes, vultures, scorpions and more. What they meant is still debated.

The hill was noticed in 1963 by a survey of Istanbul University and the University of Chicago, but the tops of the pillars were taken for gravestones. In 1994 the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt recognized what they were, and from 1995 until his death in 2014 he excavated the site with the German Archaeological Institute and the Şanlıurfa Museum. The work continues: only a small part of the hill has been dug.

Göbekli Tepe changed an old picture. Archaeologists long assumed that people first settled down and farmed, and only then built monuments; here the monuments came first, and some researchers suggest that the effort of building them helped bring people to settle. Schmidt saw the site as a sanctuary where scattered groups met for rituals. Since his death, the excavation team has found houses, thousands of grinding stones and cisterns for rainwater, and many archaeologists now see a settlement where daily life and ritual went together. The debate goes on.

UNESCO added Göbekli Tepe to the World Heritage List in 2018. Nearby hills such as Karahan Tepe hold pillars of the same kind, and the whole area is now explored as the *Taş Tepeler*, the **Stone Hills**.

blocks.tr: Göbeklitepe, Şanlıurfa'nın yakınında, bir tepenin üstünde. Büyük taşlar yaklaşık 11.600 yıldır orada. Taşların üstünde tilkiler, yılanlar ve kuşlar var. Arkeologlar 1995'ten beri burada çalışıyor. Arkeologlara göre insanlar bu taşları tarımdan önce dikti. Bunun için Göbeklitepe çok önemli.
blocks.en: Göbekli Tepe is on top of a hill near Şanlıurfa. The great stones have been there for about 11,600 years. On the stones there are foxes, snakes and birds. Archaeologists have been working here since 1995. According to archaeologists, people raised these stones before farming. That is why Göbekli Tepe is so important.

vocab.en: to raise, to put up (a stone, a post)

questions.explain: The animal bones are all from wild animals: the builders hunted and gathered.

sources.title: Göbekli Tepe
sources.note: Inscribed in 2018; in the Germuş mountains of south-eastern Anatolia; round-oval and rectangular megalithic enclosures built by hunter-gatherers between 9600 and 8200 BCE; T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.50 m, some with reliefs of belts and loincloths and of wild animals; probably used for social events and rituals

sources.title: Göbekli Tepe
sources.note: Near Şanlıurfa; investigated in the 1960s and dismissed as a medieval cemetery, recognized in the 1990s; tens of thousands of wild animal bones, mostly gazelle, and wild plant remains; foxes, scorpions, lions among the carvings; roughly 6,000 years older than Stonehenge; the building effort may have led people to settle

sources.title: Göbekli Tepe
sources.note: The 1963 survey of Istanbul University and the University of Chicago; Klaus Schmidt from 1994, excavations from 1995, his death in 2014, work continued by Istanbul University, the Şanlıurfa Museum and the German Archaeological Institute; the local Kurdish name Girê Mirazan, Wish Hill; foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and other animals in relief; later finds of domestic buildings, grinding stones and rainwater cisterns and the revised interpretation; Karahan Tepe and Taş Tepeler

sources.title: Göbeklitepe
sources.note: About 15–18 km north-east of Şanlıurfa near Örencik; about 9600–8200 BCE; excavations led by Klaus Schmidt from 1995 to 2014; the long-held ritual-centre view and the later identification of possibly residential buildings; the spelling Göbeklitepe
